title: Jean Louise Finch
text: In my [[memories]], Maycomb is full of summer light. I can still see the [[white]] houses and the trees beside the road. People sit outside after supper and talk across their gardens. A dog [[barks]]. Someone calls a child home. I remember those small sounds better than the [[names]] above the shops. They make the town feel close again.

title: Jean Louise Finch
text: Whenever I think of Maycomb, I hear a [[screen]] door closing. Clap! Then comes the soft noise of evening talk, [[drifting]] between the porches. Our street seemed [[endless]] when I was small, although I could walk its length in minutes. I remember women carrying shopping bags and men resting under trees. Their ordinary movements gave shape to my [[childhood]] world.

title: Jean Louise Finch
text: Distance has [[sharpened]] certain details of Maycomb: a grocer [[folding]] paper around a purchase, porch shadows lengthening across the steps, the [[squeak]] of a reluctant gate. Whole streets have blurred, yet these small movements remain. As a child, I thought the town contained everything worth knowing. Now I remember how confidently its inhabitants [[measured]] the world without leaving their own front yards.

title: Scout
text: The best bit of Maycomb is the road outside our house. There are trees to [[climb]] and plenty of room to run. In summer, the [[dust]] gets between my toes. I don't mind. Grown people sit on their [[porches]] and tell us to slow down, but they never go anywhere fast. Even the dogs [[sleep]] through most of the afternoon.

title: Scout
text: By lunchtime, the street is [[hot]] enough to make me hop across it. I like the shady places best, especially where tree roots push up like [[knuckles]]. You can find beetles there if nobody [[calls]] you inside. Maycomb has too many people asking where I'm going. How can I tell them? Sometimes I haven't [[decided]] until I get there.

title: Scout
text: From the courthouse steps, I can see hats [[bobbing]] through the square, each with a grown person underneath who thinks they're terribly important. Down at street level, there's better stuff: ants dragging crumbs, a loose board that [[clatters]] when I jump on it, dogs with business of their own. Adults [[complain]] that nothing happens here. I reckon they're looking too [[high]] up.

title: Jem
text: I know most of the streets in Maycomb, and I like [[showing]] the younger children around. Beyond the houses, there are [[fields]] and long roads. I'd like to follow them one day. For now, I watch the cars coming through the square. Their wheels make little clouds of [[dust]], and I try to guess how far they've [[travelled]].

title: Jem
text: Saturday brings the farmers into town, and I like watching them park their [[wagons]] near the shops. Their boots carry red [[earth]] onto the pavement. I've started noticing things like that: who has work, who buys very little, who walks home. Maycomb used to feel like one big [[playground]]. These days, I sometimes wonder what keeps the grown people so [[worried]].

title: Jem
text: A wagon wheel [[rattles]] over the uneven road, scattering the dogs outside the store. I watch the driver count his money twice before going in. Once, I'd have been [[interested]] only in the horses. Lately, the town keeps showing me things I hadn't thought to notice: [[patched]] sleeves, tired shoulders, the careful way some men ask a price before [[touching]] anything.

title: Atticus Finch
text: Before work, I enjoy the walk into town. The shops are opening, and people stop to say good [[morning]]. Some look tired, even early in the day. I try to [[listen]] when they speak. Each house has a family with its own [[worries]]. Maycomb is [[small]] enough for me to know many names, but names don't tell me everything.

title: Atticus Finch
text: There's usually someone [[waiting]] to speak to me before I reach my office. A farmer with his hat in his hands; a neighbour concerned about a fence. I don't [[hurry]] them. In a town this small, people's [[troubles]] travel the same streets as their shopping. By evening, I welcome the quiet of my [[porch]] and the sound of my children nearby.

title: Atticus Finch
text: On my morning walk, the square gradually fills with voices: shopkeepers [[exchanging]] news, farmers discussing weather, someone questioning a bill. Familiar conversations, though the [[anxiety]] beneath them deserves attention. A [[failed]] crop can enter a household long before it enters an account book. I know these streets well enough to greet their occupants; understanding what burdens each person requires rather more [[patience]].

title: Calpurnia
text: My day begins before the children are [[awake]]. Outside, Maycomb is quiet, but the kitchen soon fills with noise. [[Clink]]! A spoon [[falls]] against a pan, and somebody wants breakfast. Later, I walk past houses where other women are already working. On Sunday, I see [[friends]] at church. We talk, sing and share what we can. Those voices stay with me all week.

title: Calpurnia
text: While the town is still [[rubbing]] sleep from its eyes, I've got breakfast to prepare. Soon there'll be [[footsteps]] on the stairs and questions from the kitchen door. My working day follows the Finch family's [[needs]], but Maycomb holds my own friends and family too. At church, familiar voices rise around me, and for a while nobody is calling for their [[supper]].

title: Calpurnia
text: A kitchen window gives you a different view of Maycomb. While visitors [[admire]] tidy porches, I notice the hands that [[scrub]] the steps and carry the washing. Work leaves its marks everywhere, if you care to look. On Sundays, among my own [[congregation]], I can set those household demands aside. The singing reaches me before I've found my place, [[warm]] with familiar voices.

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Out in my [[garden]], I can hear half the street. Children run past the gate, and someone always stops for a chat. I like a little [[company]] while I work. The flowers need water in this heat, and so do I. By late afternoon, my hands are brown with earth. I [[wash]] them, then go inside to make something [[sweet]].

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Rain has a lovely way of changing Maycomb. The dusty leaves [[shine]], the earth smells [[fresh]], and all my neighbours discover [[urgent]] reasons to stay indoors. I pull on my gardening gloves and enjoy the peace. Afterwards, a few children may appear at the gate. There's generally cake in my kitchen, provided they can wait while I finish with these [[weeds]].

title: Maudie Atkinson
text: Give Maycomb a patch of bare earth and somebody will pronounce it [[hopeless]]. I prefer to fetch a [[spade]]. Even in this heat, there's pleasure in [[coaxing]] colour from stubborn soil while bees bustle between the flowers. By afternoon, neighbours lean over my fence with advice I haven't requested. I let them talk, [[pinch]] away a dead bloom, and carry on planting.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: You can learn a lot from my front [[porch]]. The shops are close, so nearly everyone walks past my house. I notice new hats, dirty shoes and people who look [[upset]]. Sometimes I call them over for a talk. It's good to know your [[neighbours]]. Besides, if a strange car stops in our street, somebody should [[find]] out why.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: Well, there goes another visitor to the house across the street. A [[cousin]], perhaps, although nobody [[mentioned]] a cousin yesterday. From my porch, I keep an eye on these things. Maycomb looks [[quiet]] to strangers, but that's because they don't know where to look. By supper, I'll probably have the whole story. Mrs Atkinson might know something; she's usually [[outside]] with her flowers.

title: Stephanie Crawford
text: There are people who call Maycomb [[uneventful]]. I can only suppose they spend their afternoons asleep. Before breakfast, I've noticed a [[borrowed]] motorcar, an unfamiliar parcel and a neighbour wearing her Sunday hat on a [[Tuesday]]. None of it proves anything, naturally. Still, I move my chair a little nearer the porch [[rail]], where the view of the street is considerably better.

title: Mrs Dubose
text: From my chair, I can see the road and my [[roses]]. The flowers look better than most of the children who pass this house. Dirty faces, loud voices, no [[manners]]. I tell them so. A proper town needs people who care about these things. Now and then, someone stops and speaks [[politely]]. I [[enjoy]] that, though I don't always say it.

title: Mrs Dubose
text: [[Scrape]], scrape. Another pair of shoes [[dragged]] past my gate. Does nobody teach children to lift their feet? I sit among my roses and watch Maycomb grow [[careless]]. Hats stay on when they ought to come off, and young people answer before you've finished speaking. At least my garden still shows what attention can do. I move my chair further into the [[shade]].

title: Mrs Dubose
text: My porch gives me a clear view of the street, though what passes for behaviour there gives me little [[satisfaction]]. Children [[shriek]]; men neglect to remove their hats. I haven't spent a lifetime learning proper behaviour to watch it disappear without comment. Beneath the rail, my roses hold their heads up. Their [[scent]] reaches me whenever the air [[stirs]], and I settle deeper into my chair.

title: Nathan Radley
text: I like our gate [[closed]]. People in Maycomb ask too many [[questions]], especially when a house is quiet. There's work to do here, just as there is anywhere else. I [[clear]] the yard and check the fence. Beyond it, children shout and neighbours talk. I can [[hear]] them perfectly well. That doesn't mean I need to open the door.

title: Nathan Radley
text: The [[hedge]] needs cutting again. I work along it slowly, hearing footsteps [[pause]] on the other side. In Maycomb, a quiet household gives people something to discuss, and ours seems to interest them more than most. Let them talk. There's [[comfort]] in a straight fence and a gate that shuts properly. When I've finished outside, I put the [[tools]] away and go in.

title: Nathan Radley
text: Neighbours mistake [[privacy]] for a reason to invent stories. I've lived long enough in Maycomb to recognise that habit, and I see no reason to [[encourage]] it. Along our fence, I check a loose board and press the gate against its [[latch]]. Beyond the hedge, conversation stops for a moment. By the time it starts again, I'm [[carrying]] my tools towards the back of the house.

title: Boo Radley
text: I hear Maycomb before I see it. Wheels pass the house, and birds [[sing]] in the trees outside. When children run along the road, their voices come through the [[window]]. I listen until they are gone. At night, everything is [[softer]]. A dog moves near the fence. Leaves [[touch]] the wall. I know many small sounds in this quiet room.

title: Boo Radley
text: Through a narrow space beside the [[curtain]], I can watch the light move across the street. Morning brings footsteps, carts and voices I [[recognise]] without seeing their faces. Later, the heat empties the road. A bird lands on our fence and [[tilts]] its head towards the house. I stay still. For a moment, we watch each other through the [[dusty]] glass.

title: Boo Radley
text: The town reaches my room in pieces: a wheel striking a stone, kitchen smoke [[drifting]] through a gap, laughter passing and fading. I put these fragments together until I can almost follow the street beyond my window. Towards evening, [[shadows]] join beneath the trees. Fewer eyes outside then. I stand a little [[closer]] to the glass and watch a small [[moth]] settle there.

title: Dill
text: Every house in Maycomb looks like the start of a story. A dark window? There could be a secret room behind it. A broken gate? Perhaps someone [[escaped]] last night. I like to walk [[slowly]] and look at everything. The other children know these streets already, but I keep [[finding]] new things. Even a strange [[noise]] can give me an idea.

title: Dill
text: Maycomb's got enough stories for a hundred summers, if you ask me. I can turn a [[crooked]] tree into a giant and a locked shed into a pirate's store. The others say I'm making things up. Well, of course I am! By evening, when the porches [[glow]] and families call their children home, I sometimes wish I [[belonged]] to one of those [[pictures]].

title: Dill
text: Summer makes a [[stage]] of Maycomb. Behind every curtain, I imagine a secret; down every lane, an adventure waiting for its leading man. Naturally, I [[volunteer]]. The town is generous with [[scenery]]: leaning fences, mysterious gardens, sheds that deserve investigation. Then a mother calls from a doorway, and the other children drift home. I linger beneath the trees, [[rehearsing]] something splendid to tell them tomorrow.

title: Heck Tate
text: Most mornings, I walk around the square and speak to the [[shopkeepers]]. They tell me about broken windows, missing things and [[dogs]] that won't stay home. I [[listen]]. Usually, the town is quiet, but I still look down the side streets. By evening, I know which shops are closed and which lights are [[burning]]. It's part of being the sheriff.

title: Heck Tate
text: From a distance, Maycomb looks [[peaceful]] enough: wagons by the stores, men [[exchanging]] news, children under everybody's feet. I know which voices to listen for. A sudden shout can mean nothing; two men speaking too [[quietly]] may need watching. Mostly, though, my rounds bring ordinary [[complaints]]. I stop outside a shop, adjust my hat and hear about another broken fence.

title: Heck Tate
text: A sheriff learns to read the square by its small [[disturbances]]. One shop opening late; a horse left [[restless]] at the rail; conversation stopping as I approach. Most mean nothing serious, but I notice them all the same. Under the [[awnings]], men debate weather and money while wagons [[grind]] past. I exchange a greeting, pause for an answer, then continue towards the next doorway.

title: Judge Taylor
text: The courthouse is a good place to watch Maycomb. From a [[window]], I can see people crossing the square with bags and baskets. Their voices [[rise]] through the warm air. Inside, papers wait on my desk. I take off my [[glasses]] and [[rub]] my eyes. Outside, a man stops to talk. His horse must wait, and so must my work.

title: Judge Taylor
text: By mid-afternoon, the heat has settled over the courthouse like a thick [[blanket]]. I [[loosen]] my collar and listen to a fly [[quarrelling]] with the window. Down below, Maycomb carries on at its usual pace. A wagon rolls past; two neighbours begin a conversation neither seems likely to finish. The papers on my desk haven't moved either. I reach for my [[glasses]].

title: Judge Taylor
text: Official business has its hours; Maycomb has its own arrangements. From my courthouse window, I watch a man abandon an [[errand]] for a conversation that could comfortably outlast both. Heat [[gathers]] beneath the roof, and a fly conducts an energetic [[inspection]] of my desk. I remove my glasses, rub the bridge of my nose, and allow the town another minute before returning to its [[paperwork]].

title: Reverend Sykes
text: On Sunday mornings, I hear people coming towards our church. Some walk a long way, and their shoes are covered in [[dust]]. We open the [[doors]] to let in the air. Soon the room is full of faces I know. I see tired people [[smiling]] at their friends. When we sing, the sound grows strong enough to fill every quiet [[corner]].

title: Reverend Sykes
text: Our church stands beyond the comfortable streets that visitors usually admire. I know the families who walk here, carrying a week's tiredness in their [[shoulders]]. Before the service, we share news of work, [[illness]] and children. Someone always needs help, and someone usually has a little to [[give]]. Then the singing begins. Beside the open door, I hear the whole room [[breathe]] together.

title: Reverend Sykes
text: Long before I begin the service, the [[congregation]] tells me how well Maycomb is managing. An empty seat, a worried glance, a quiet question about work: each asks for [[attention]]. Outside, dust [[whitens]] the shoes of late arrivals. Inside, neighbours make room along the benches. When the singing rises, I hear familiar voices supporting one another, the [[uncertain]] ones gradually finding their strength among the rest.

title: Helen Robinson
text: I like the time just before [[supper]], when our neighbours come outside. Children play near the houses, and women [[call]] across the road. I can put down my work for a few minutes. There are [[worries]], of course, but there is [[laughter]] too. A friend asks how I am, and I tell her. In our part of Maycomb, that matters.

title: Helen Robinson
text: My children can find a [[game]] in almost anything: a stick, an empty box, a patch of shade. I watch them while I finish the [[washing]]. Beyond our houses, Maycomb has gardens and shop windows that seem to [[belong]] to another world. Here, a neighbour calls out an offer of help. I smile back, then spread another [[damp]] shirt between my hands.

title: Helen Robinson
text: There are afternoons when Maycomb seems to measure out its [[comforts]] street by street. Beyond our neighbourhood, gardens are planted for pleasure; here, every scrap of ground must [[earn]] its keep. Yet warmth travels easily between our [[doorways]]. A neighbour watches the children while I finish a chore. Later, I carry over something from our kitchen and stay to talk as the light [[fades]].

title: Mayella Ewell
text: Town looks pretty from a long way off. I can see trees around the houses, and I think about the clean rooms [[inside]]. Near our place, there's [[rubbish]] beside the road. The little children make a lot of noise. I try to [[grow]] a few flowers because I like looking at something nice. Their [[bright]] heads turn towards the sun.

title: Mayella Ewell
text: Sometimes I look towards town and imagine a house where every chair has its own place. There'd be clean [[curtains]], perhaps, and [[nobody]] stepping over things on the floor. Here, the children shout and the smell of rubbish [[hangs]] in the heat. I water my flowers [[carefully]]. They're small, but their colour catches my eye whenever I come through the yard.

title: Mayella Ewell
text: From our end of the road, Maycomb's respectable houses seem [[impossibly]] complete: fences without [[gaps]], curtains that match, front steps someone has time to [[scrub]]. I wonder what it feels like to open a door without wanting to hide what's behind it. Rubbish shifts in the ditch outside our yard. I turn towards my flowers, [[touching]] a leaf to see whether they need water.

title: Bob Ewell
text: Those men in town like to stand outside the shops and look [[important]]. I know what they think when I [[walk]] past. Let them look. Their houses might be bigger than mine, but they don't own every [[road]] in Maycomb. I go where I please. At our end of town, there's room to spit without somebody telling you how to [[behave]].

title: Bob Ewell
text: There's a certain way the [[shopkeepers]] watch a man when his clothes aren't good enough for them. I've seen it often. They stand behind their [[counters]] as if a clean shirt makes them kings. Well, I won't [[bow]] to the lot of them. Out by our place, dogs [[nose]] through rubbish and children kick up dust. Nobody there tells me where to stand.

title: Bob Ewell
text: Fine houses, polished shoes, neighbours forever [[judging]] a man's fence. That's Maycomb for you. Walk into a store without money and watch the welcome [[cool]]. I know I'm poor; I still expect the respect [[due]] a white man. Beyond the neat streets, rubbish [[smokes]] beside the road to our place. I kick a bottle out of my path and leave it where it lands.

title: Mr Gilmer
text: When work brings me to Maycomb, I go straight to the [[square]]. The courthouse is easy to find, and most of the shops are [[nearby]]. People stop to talk more than I would like. I prefer to finish my [[business]] first. Still, I notice who says [[hello]] and who looks away. A small town can tell you quite a lot.

title: Mr Gilmer
text: Maycomb always seems to have time for another conversation. I arrive with papers to sort, yet somebody wants to discuss a neighbour's family before I've taken off my [[hat]]. [[Names]] matter here, perhaps more than they should. I listen all the same. By the time I reach the courthouse, I've learnt who owns the store, who [[owes]] money and who expects [[attention]].

title: Mr Gilmer
text: For a visiting lawyer, Maycomb requires a certain amount of listening before any useful business begins. Family connections are explained, old disagreements [[revived]], introductions prolonged. I keep my [[impatience]] behind a polite expression. Around the square, influence announces itself quietly: a shopkeeper leaving his [[counter]] to greet one customer, barely looking up at another. Such [[distinctions]] are worth remembering when one works here.

title: Tom Robinson
text: Early in the morning, I walk past the fields while the air is still [[cool]]. Birds move in the long [[grass]], and I can smell the earth. Later, town gets busy. I speak [[politely]] and keep out of people's way. At home, the children run to [[meet]] me. Their voices are the sound I like best in all of Maycomb.

title: Tom Robinson
text: I know the roads around Maycomb by the dust they leave on my [[boots]]. Work takes me past fields, fences and houses where I wouldn't be welcome inside. I watch my step and mind my words. Near home, I can walk a little [[easier]]. Someone's [[cooking]], children are laughing, and Helen [[lifts]] her face when she hears me at the door.

title: Tom Robinson
text: [[Dawn]] gives the roads a brief gentleness. I walk towards work while mist hangs over the fields, before the heat and the watching eyes gather. In town, I pay [[attention]] to how close I stand and how quickly I answer. Those [[habits]] follow me home, but loosen there. Hearing the children call, I lift my good hand in greeting and lengthen my [[stride]].

title: Mr Cunningham
text: I come into Maycomb when there's something I need for the [[farm]]. The shops have plenty of things I can't buy, so I don't [[spend]] long looking. A bag of [[seed]] matters more than a new coat. Once my business is done, I'm glad to leave. Out beyond the houses, I can watch the [[sky]] and think about the weather.

title: Mr Cunningham
text: The square [[smells]] of horses, hot dust and things for sale. I bring my list, count my money and try to keep the two in [[agreement]]. Nobody needs to tell me times are hard. You can see it in the farmers' [[patched]] coats. Once I've bought what I can, I head home. There's a [[field]] waiting that won't care how I look.

title: Mr Cunningham
text: Before setting out for Maycomb, I work out what the farm can [[afford]]. The answer rarely fills a shopping bag. Around the square, other men make similar [[calculations]], [[turning]] a tool over before asking its price. We discuss rain instead of money; it's easier. By late afternoon, I welcome the road home, where the smell of worked earth [[replaces]] the dust of the stores.
